newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour gears up to get out big election vote. [CORRECTED 20:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: UK Labour gears up to get out big election vote. [CORRECTED 20:00 GMT]

text.p: Tony Blair's Labour party, confident but not complacent about forming Britain's government for the first time in 18 years, plans to mobilise half a million supporters to maximise its vote in Thursday's election.

Aides to Blair, disclosing the plans to move up a final gear for the end of the marathon six-week campaign, on Tuesday dismissed polls showing the main opposition party as much as 20 percentage points ahead of the ruling Conservatives.
"I take nothing for granted -- not one seat not one vote," Blair said in Bristol, western England. "I intend to work flat out for every vote, every ounce of trust, every bit of support."
Prime Minister John Major also mounted a final push, warning that a vote for Labour was a "one-way bet" for higher taxes and an end to the prosperity his government had brought about.

Taking a Conservative defeat for granted, newspapers speculated on how quickly Major would step down as party leader and whether the prime minister's flat at 10 Downing Street would have to be extended to make it big enough for Blair's three children.
But a defiant Major insisted the race was still open and said he was going all out to ensure a fifth Conservative victory in a row in Thursday's ballot.
Major showed his frustration that his party was not reaping more credit for falling unemployment (corrects from employment) and rising living standards.
Speaking in Brighton, southern England, he said that when Labour gave up power in 1979 Britain had a "basket case economy". Now it was the best-performer in Europe.
"All the things we did to achieve it, they (Labour) stood against and opposed day after day after day," Major said.

He said Labour, which has co-opted many of the Conservatives' policies in a bid to woo middle-class voters, had "an astonishing piece of brass-necked effrontery" to claim it could run the economy more effectively than his own government.
Major also said Blair was guilty of "truly unscrupulous untruths" in claiming the Conservatives would put tax on food and scrap the state pension if they were re-elected.
"I believe they have truly stepped into the gutter of public life," Major told a meeting of party workers and pensioners.
The prime minister could be forgiven for being testy. He had woken to newspaper headlines saying he would announce his decision to step down within hours of what was likely to be a crushing defeat.

"I will quit as leader," the pro-Conservative Daily Express trumpeted on its front page. The Financial Times, which on Thursday gave lukewarm backing to Blair, said Major was under pressure to hang on until the autumn because an immediate leadership election could tear the party apart.
Major brushed aside all talk of defeat and disunity, saying many voters were still undecided.

He said people would judge the government on its five-year record. Measured by inflation, unemployment, growth in living standards, competitiveness or any other standard, Britain was clearly in far better shape than it was in 1979 or 1992.
"I believe people will make up their mind, in a mature democracy, on the record of that has happened and perhaps most relevantly of all, in the plans for the future," he said.

Labour, which needs a 4.3 percent swing to win power, was 22 points ahead in a poll in Tuesday's Daily Telegraph. But Labour strategists said their private surveys had never pointed to a 15-point lead, let alone a landslide margin of 20 points.
"The election is a lot closer than you people think," one aide told reporters.
Blair on Tuesday rammed home his main message that Labour's limited but precise commitments would make a difference.

"This is my contract with the British people -- my bond of trust with them. I ask them to judge me and us upon it, hold me to it. The buck will stop with me. What I promise, I will deliver," Blair said.
